groups.text:
For each question from 16 to 20, choose the word(s) closest in meaning to the underlined word(s).

Caring for a dog has many wonderful benefits. Dogs provide companionship, which helps to __(16: alleviate)__ feelings of loneliness and stress. Studies have shown that petting a dog for just ten minutes can have a significant impact on reducing anxiety levels. Dogs also encourage more physical activity among dog owners as they have to take them on __(17: regular)__ walks. Fellow dog owners can also bond and connect over __(18: anecdotes)__ of their dogs' quirky behaviours.
However, it is important to remember that looking after a dog is __(19: no walk in the park)__. Before deciding to bring a dog into your home, make sure you are __(20: completely)__ prepared to commit to their needs for many years. It would be wise for prospective dog owners to consider their lifestyle, schedules and budget before making such a commitment.
Adapted from American Kennel Club

For each question from 21 to 25, choose the best answer.

The extract below is taken from an online article.
School bags are designed to be both roomy and trendy, which makes them appealing to students. Lately, more focus has been put on making school bags look good. Many students use their school bags as a way to express their personality and personal style. Is that true for you, too?
While it may seem exciting to fit everything into one bag, have you considered the weight? Carrying too many items strains your back. This may cause short-term discomfort and lead to long-term posture problems. To cushion the effect, you should carry a school bag that fits comfortably on your back. Features such as wide straps and padded backs help distribute weight more evenly. By choosing a school bag wisely, you can reduce the pressure on your back.
Ultimately, health experts recommend packing only the items needed for the day to keep your school bag light. For example, you can store certain items in your school locker or keep some materials under your desk if your school allows it. By planning what you bring each day and leaving out unnecessary items, you can protect your back and still have everything you need.

images.alt: Poster for a school bag, with a photo of a backpack in the middle. Text: Peaks School Bag. Carry Everything in Style. Say goodbye to boring school bags! Fit your entire school day into one bag – all your books, stationery, lunch boxes and more! Get organised with a specific space for everything! No more mess or things left behind! Suitable for students of all ages! Wide range of colours to choose from! Big bags never felt so comfortable! Beside a photo of a schoolboy carrying the bag: "I love my Peaks bag. Although it's bigger than other school bags, I bought it because it's extremely comfortable. Everything I need for school fits inside it. I can also find any item easily! – Ansel, 12-year-old student

groups.text:
There are 10 blanks, numbered 26 to 35, in the passage below. From the list of words given, choose the most suitable word for each blank. Write its letter (A to Q) in the blank. The letters (I) and (O) have been omitted to avoid confusion during marking.
**EACH WORD CAN BE USED ONLY ONCE.**
[[table1]]

Last Saturday, our school gardening club visited a community farm. For months, the club members __(26)__ been learning how vegetables are grown in small spaces.
At the farm, we were divided into several groups so that __(27)__ team could try a different activity. My group was asked to loosen the soil gently __(28)__ the roots were delicate. Next, the farmer showed us a tool with a short handle __(29)__ was safer for children to use.
He reminded us that we __(30)__ not pour too much water onto the plants. Too little water would dry them out, __(31)__ too much water would drown them. __(32)__ the end of the session, we harvested spinach and placed the stalks carefully into baskets.
The baskets carried by our group were heavier __(33)__ the rest because we had picked vegetables from twice as many rows compared to others. Before leaving, we thanked the farmer, who told us to wash __(34)__ hands before eating anything. We also learnt that fresh produce often tastes better __(35)__ it is eaten soon after harvesting. The visit made many of us eager to start a small class garden.

Each of the underlined words contains either a spelling or grammatical error. Write the correct word in each of the boxes.

Last month, our class organised an exhibition about how neighbourhoods in Singapore have changed over time. Our teacher reminded us that everyone __(36: have)__ an important role to play. She also said that a panel would be put near the entrance to __(37: comemoret)__ the pioneers who had contributed to the estate.
The hall was already buzzing __(38: in)__ activity on the morning of the exhibition. Every display board __(39: were)__ checked very carefully before the visitors arrived. A few of us were still making minor changes as we wanted the information to be both accurate and __(40: coherant)__. Later, a resident of more than fifty years noticed an old photograph of a market and told us that he had __(41: wrote)__ about the same place many years earlier in his __(42: jornal)__.
At the far end of the hall stood a table of artefacts that families had kindly lent to the school. They were not __(43: asppecialy)__ valuable but helped us imagine what daily life had once been like. __(44: Since)__ being tired after clearing up, many of us felt that the effort had been __(45: undoubtably)__ worthwhile. The exhibition taught us that even ordinary objects can tell meaningful stories about the past.

Fill in each blank with a suitable word.

Have you ever noticed how some children can remember facts better after turning them into a game? At our school, a group of teachers have begun using a new approach to teaching by adding short revision games to their lessons. __(46)__ of copying notes for the entire period, students now work in small __(47)__ to answer questions, sort cards and explain ideas to one another.
When students discuss possible answers, they must listen closely and think carefully about __(48)__ their ideas make sense to others. This helps them to reflect on their answers and spot any mistakes before __(49)__ them with the class. The games may also encourage quieter students to join in. They can first discuss in small groups before speaking to the whole class. __(50)__ gives them time to build their confidence step by step. In one activity, students are given clue cards to arrange in the correct __(51)__ to show how a process works. In a different activity, they earn points by __(52)__ why one answer is wrong while another is correct. Such tasks take only a few minutes, but they keep students alert and fully focused during the lesson. Teachers have noticed that after taking part in such activities, students are __(53)__ willing to ask questions. This may be because the games __(54)__ learning feel less stressful.
Of course, revision games are beneficial only __(55)__ students continue to revise their notes and complete their homework. Fun activities can support learning, but teachers and students __(56)__ should understand that the use of such activities in lessons __(57)__ just one part of the learning process, not the whole of it. A balanced routine, with time set __(58)__ for reading, practice and discussion, is more often than __(59)__ the most effective way to prepare for an examination. When students enjoy the process of learning, they are more likely to stay __(60)__ task. Used wisely, revision games can make learning enjoyable and worth looking forward to too.

Read the passage and answer questions 66 to 75.

**1** When I was in Secondary Two, my form teacher once told me, in front of the whole class, that I was "the sort of girl who could not fit anywhere". The words were spoken lightly, almost carelessly, but they stayed with me long after the lesson ended. For the rest of the day, I carried a quiet heaviness in me, even as everyone else laughed and chatted as though nothing had happened.
**2** At assemblies, we were supposed to line up neatly, socks pulled up, hair tied properly, badges pinned straight. Everyone around me seemed to know how to **turn themselves into the shape the school wanted**. I, unlike the others, had my shirt tucked out and dirty shoes. My shoelaces were two different shades of blue because I had replaced one missing lace with whatever I could find. To make things worse, I had been caught drawing a strange shape in the margin of the school newsletter instead of reading it. "What is that?" my form teacher had asked sharply, holding up **my paper**. I stared at the page. I had drawn a blob with uneven edges and tiny arms stretching out. "An amoeba," I muttered. A few girls giggled. "Exactly," she said. "A single-celled organism with no proper shape. Just floating about aimlessly. That is your problem."
**3** From that day on, the words followed me everywhere. Amoeba girl. Blob. Floating aimlessly. It did not help that I asked too many questions when I was supposed to accept instructions. When the others talked excitedly about becoming doctors, lawyers or scholars, I stayed silent because none of those dreams felt like mine. I liked watching people instead, noticing the way they performed a version of themselves for the world.
**4** At home, things were not much easier. "Can you do what you are told?" Mother often scolded. "Why can't you be more like your cousin? She knows how to behave." "There she goes again!" I thought bitterly as I walked away from this familiar rant. I did know how to behave. I simply could not bear pretending for too long. Since then, I began to think of myself as an amoeba. Not the insult my teacher had intended, but the real creature I had seen under a microscope in the science lab. It had no neat outline, no fixed form, and yet it was alive. It moved. It survived. On my worst days, I was exactly like that, a strange little blob drifting quietly through school, unseen and unimportant.
**5** Then, one afternoon, something changed. It was the final week of the term. My class was engrossed in playing board games, gossiping and laughing with one another. This was interrupted by our teacher who gave us instructions to create a short performance about good behaviour. Most of my classmates **groaned and did the bare minimum**. As they argued lazily over the script, hoping to get it over with, I suddenly felt something stir inside me. Before I could stop myself, the words slipped out. "This is boring," I said. "No one will listen." My heart thumped in my chest as I took over the script. This was something I never imagined myself doing. I began rewriting the whole scene. In half an hour, I completed **the task**. I made the dialogue sharper and funnier. I showed them where to stand and when to pause. Somehow, everyone listened. Even the loudest girls followed my instructions.
**6** During the performance, the audience laughed at the right moments. For the first time in school, I was not being stared at because I was wrong. I was being watched because I had made something people could feel. Afterwards, our English teacher came up to me. "You wrote most of that, didn't you?" she asked. I nodded, expecting criticism. Instead, she smiled. "You notice things other people miss. That is **a gift**. You should do something with it."
**7** As we packed up our props, the same girls who had groaned earlier now lingered by my desk. One of them, the loudest in the group, smiled awkwardly and asked if I would help her with her drama club audition the following week. This caught me completely off guard. Just days ago, she had been rolling her eyes at my mismatched shoelaces. Now, she was looking at me not as a joke, but as an expert. I agreed, feeling a strange warmth spread through my chest.
**8** That night, I drew an amoeba again. But this time, I saw a creature that could adapt and find its own way forward. Perhaps not fitting in did not mean I was broken; it simply meant I was still forming. I began to imagine myself writing and directing plays. Maybe one day, these would reach a fellow amoeba who needed to know that she was not alone.
Adapted from How Tan Siyou turned rebellion into new film 'Amoeba' by The Straits Times

questions.stem:
The pictures below show Ricky and his classmate, Alice, discussing an idea during their school recess. Study the pictures carefully.
[[img1]]
++Your Task++
Imagine you are Ricky.
**Write an email to your principal, Mdm Tan, asking her to consider setting up a reading corner.**
You are to refer to the pictures and information above for your email. The bullet point underlined below requires you to come up with your own information.

In your writing, include the following key information:
- why you think a reading corner should be set up
- where the reading corner can be set up
- two ways you can contribute
- how your schoolmates may contribute
- ++one suggestion on how to make the reading corner more attractive to students++
You may reorder the points. Remember to write in complete sentences.

images.alt: Two comic panels showing Alice and Ricky from behind, standing outside the school LIBRARY, where students are reading at a full table; a staircase is on the right and there is an empty space between the library and the staircase. Panel 1. Alice: 'Ricky, there are no empty seats in the school library again!' Ricky: 'It's getting harder for avid readers like us to find a quiet, comfortable place to sit and read during recess. Hmm... Look over there, Alice. Don't you think the vacant space between the library and the staircase would be perfect for a reading corner?' Alice: 'You're right!' Panel 2. Ricky: 'I can provide an old bookshelf which is still in good condition. My parents have been thinking of giving it away. I can also design some posters to decorate the reading corner. Students can even donate their pre-loved books for others to read.' Alice: 'Wow, those are great ideas! You should email our principal with your suggestion.' Ricky: 'Thanks, Alice! I'll do that after checking with my parents.'

answer.value: There is no single model answer. Check your writing against the points below.

explanation: Purpose: to ask (persuade) the principal to consider setting up a reading corner. Say this clearly in the opening lines and repeat the request politely at the end.

Audience: Mdm Tan, your principal. Context: you are Ricky, a pupil of the school. Use a formal, respectful tone: 'Dear Mdm Tan', no slang or short forms, and a polite close such as 'Thank you for considering my suggestion.' Sign off 'Yours sincerely, Ricky' and give your class.
Point 1, why: there are often no empty seats in the school library, so it is getting harder for avid readers to find a quiet, comfortable place to sit and read during recess.
Point 2, where: the vacant space between the library and the staircase.

Point 3, two ways you can contribute: provide an old bookshelf that is still in good condition (your parents have been thinking of giving it away), and design some posters to decorate the reading corner.
Point 4, how schoolmates may contribute: they can donate their pre-loved books for others to read.

Point 5, your own idea (the underlined point): one sensible suggestion to make the corner more attractive, for example adding cushions or beanbags, displaying a 'Book of the Week', or letting classes take turns to decorate it. The picture does not give this, so you must think of it yourself.

Format and accuracy: email layout (To, From, Subject, greeting, paragraphs, sign-off). Write as 'I' (Ricky), not 'Ricky said'. Do not copy the speech bubbles word for word; change them into your own complete sentences. Marks are for task fulfilment (all five points, purpose, audience, context) and for language.

review.keyAnswer: No model answer in the key.

questions.stem:
Write a composition of ++at least 150 words++ about **making something better.**
The pictures are provided to help you think about this topic.
Your composition must be based on one or more of these pictures.
[[img1]]
Consider the following points when you plan your composition:
- What had to be made better?
- How did it get better?
You may use the points in any order and include other relevant points as well.

images.alt: Three pictures, one above the other. Picture 1: a boy and a younger child at a stall with cupcakes and a cake; the sign on the stall says 'Charity Bake Sale'. Picture 2: an empty stage with a stool and a microphone on a stand. Picture 3: a beach littered with rubbish: tied rubbish bags, plastic bottles, cans and food boxes on the sand near the water.

answer.value: There is no single model answer. Check your writing against the points below.

explanation: Understand the topic: 'making something better' means something was not good enough at first, and someone's effort improved it. Your story must show clearly what was wrong (before), what was done, and how it was better (after).

Picture 1, the charity bake sale: the bakes tasted bad or sales were poor at first, and you improved the recipe, the display or the teamwork so that more money was raised. It could also be about making other people's lives better through the money raised.

Picture 2, the stage with a stool and microphone: a weak speech, song or performance that got better through practice and feedback, or stage fright that you overcame. You could also make a dull school concert better.
Picture 3, the littered beach: a dirty beach made better by a clean-up that you organised or joined, or people's careless habits changed for the better.

Story arc: (1) opening that shows the problem; (2) the moment you decided something had to change; (3) what you did, including a setback or difficulty so that the improvement is not too easy; (4) the result, shown through what people saw, said and felt.
Answer both guiding points in the story: what had to be made better, and how it got better. Use at least one picture and keep the topic at the centre from start to finish, not only in the last line.
Ending: return to the topic with a reflection, for example what you learnt about effort, patience or working together to make something better.
Language: at least 150 words (aim for much more), paragraphs, past tense kept consistent, varied sentence openings, and vivid words to show feelings and actions.

review.keyAnswer: No model answer in the key.
review.solvedAnswer: Planning checklist written from the task.

questions.stem: Sam and his groupmates __________ their group project, but they will only submit it next week.

explanation: First find the subject: 'Sam **and** his groupmates'. Two subjects joined by 'and' are plural, so the helping verb is 'have', not 'has'. That removes options (1) and (3).
Next choose the tense. The project is already finished, because they are only waiting to submit it. A finished action with a result now takes the present perfect: have + past participle.
'have been completing' is tempting, but the present perfect continuous means the action is still going on, which does not fit a project that is ready to be submitted.
'Sam and his groupmates have completed their group project.' The answer is option (2).

questions.stem: You __________ take better care of your belongings or they might go missing.

explanation: The sentence gives advice and a warning: do this, 'or they might go missing'.
Rule: use 'should' to give advice or to say what is the right thing to do.
'can' and 'could' only say that something is possible or that you are able to do it. 'would' is for imagined situations or polite requests. None of them gives advice.
'You should take better care of your belongings.' The answer is option (4).

questions.stem: If I had known about the book sale, I __________ you there.

explanation: Look at the 'if' part: 'If I **had known**'. This is the past perfect, so the speaker is imagining a past that did not happen (he did not know about the sale).
Rule (third conditional): If + past perfect, ... would have + past participle.
'would follow' is tempting, but it goes with 'If I knew' (second conditional), which is about now or the future, not the past.
'If I had known about the book sale, I would have followed you there.' The answer is option (4).

questions.stem: We are going to be late, so I suggest we cut __________ this field to get to the bus stop.

explanation: Clue: they are late, so they want the shortest way to the bus stop.
'cut across' a place means to go straight through it from one side to the other as a shortcut, instead of going round it.
'around' is the opposite of a shortcut. 'cut into' means to slice something or to interrupt, and 'cut over' is not used for taking a shortcut.
'...we cut across this field to get to the bus stop.' The answer is option (3).

questions.stem: Having won the tournament, my teammates and I treated __________ to a feast.

explanation: Ask who did the treating and who received the treat. Both are the same people: 'my teammates and I'.
Rule: when the subject and the object are the same people, use a reflexive pronoun (a '-self' or '-selves' word).
'My teammates and I' is the same as 'we', and the reflexive pronoun for 'we' is 'ourselves'. 'themselves' goes with 'they', and 'us' is not reflexive.
'...my teammates and I treated ourselves to a feast.' The answer is option (3).

questions.stem: One-fifth of the students __________ absent from school yesterday.

explanation: 'yesterday' tells us the verb must be in the past tense, so 'is' and 'are' are out.
Rule: with a fraction + 'of', the verb agrees with the noun after 'of'. 'One-fifth of the students' is a number of students, and 'students' is plural, so the verb is plural.
'was' is tempting because of the word 'One', but it would only be right with something that cannot be counted, such as 'One-fifth of the cake was eaten.'
'One-fifth of the students were absent from school yesterday.' The answer is option (4).

questions.stem: As I was returning home from school, I heard a dog __________ loudly.

explanation: Rule: after a verb of the senses (see, hear, watch, feel, notice) + object, use the -ing form (or the base form) of the next verb: heard + a dog + barking.
'barking' shows the dog was in the middle of barking when I heard it.

'was barking' is tempting, but 'heard' is already the main verb of this clause. 'I heard a dog was barking' would need 'that' and has a different meaning. 'barked' gives the clause two main verbs, and 'had barking' is not a real verb form.
'...I heard a dog barking loudly.' The answer is option (2).

questions.stem: We visited the museum __________ the rare fossil bones are displayed.

explanation: The blank begins a clause that tells us more about 'the museum', which is a place.
The clause after the blank is already complete: 'the rare fossil bones are displayed'. It tells us what happens **in** that place, so we need 'where' (= in which).
'which' is tempting because a museum is a thing, but then we would have to say 'in which the bones are displayed' or 'which displays the bones'. 'whom' is for people and 'whose' shows belonging.
'We visited the museum where the rare fossil bones are displayed.' The answer is option (3).

questions.stem: He'll want you to accompany him, __________ he?

explanation: Rule: a positive statement takes a negative question tag, and the tag uses the same helping verb as the statement.
'He'll' is short for 'He **will**'. The helping verb is 'will', and its negative is 'won't'.
'wouldn't' is tempting, but it goes with 'He'd' (he would). 'doesn't' and 'didn't' go with statements that have no helping verb, such as 'He wants' or 'He wanted'.
'He'll want you to accompany him, won't he?' The answer is option (1).

questions.stem: "Please move __________ pairs of shoes here to that corner," my teacher said to me.

explanation: Two clues decide the word: how many, and how near.
'pairs' is plural, so we need a plural word: 'these' or 'those'. That removes 'this' and 'that'.
The shoes are 'here', near the speaker, so we use 'these'. 'those' is for things that are far away, like 'that corner'.
'Please move these pairs of shoes here to that corner.' The answer is option (3).

questions.stem: After weeks of __________ by the owner, the leaves of the young plant withered and it died shortly after.

explanation: Clues: the leaves 'withered' and the plant 'died', and the blank is something done 'by the owner'.
'neglect' means not giving something the care it needs. A plant that is not watered or looked after will wither and die.

'deterioration' (becoming worse) is tempting, but it happens to the plant; it is not something the owner does to it. 'disrepair' is used for buildings and machines in bad condition, and 'nourishment' (food needed to grow) would keep the plant alive.
The answer is option (1), neglect.

questions.stem: Try not to let the difficult questions __________ you and stop you from attempting the other simpler ones.

explanation: Clue: the difficult questions might 'stop you from attempting' the easier ones. We need a word for making someone too scared or unsure to try.
'intimidate' means to frighten someone so that they lose confidence.

'aggravate' is tempting, but it means to make a problem worse or to annoy someone; being annoyed would not stop you from trying easier questions. 'subdue' means to bring under control by force, and 'excite' is a positive feeling.
The answer is option (3), intimidate.

questions.stem: These musicians have an __________ way of making music using pots and pans.

explanation: Clue: they make music 'using pots and pans', not normal instruments. We need a word that means unusual, not done the normal way.
'unconventional' means different from what is usual or traditional.
'unassuming' means modest and not showing off; 'unbecoming' means not suitable or not proper; 'unfazed' means not worried or upset. These describe people or behaviour, not an unusual method.
The answer is option (4), unconventional.

questions.stem: My father knocked __________ on my sister's door as she was going to be late for school.

explanation: Clue: she 'was going to be late', so Father kept knocking and would not stop until she responded.
'insistently' means again and again, in a way that demands attention.

'compulsively' is tempting, but it means being unable to stop doing something because of a habit you cannot control, not because of a good reason. 'laboriously' means with great effort and slowly; 'persuasively' means in a way that convinces someone with words.
The answer is option (1), insistently.

questions.stem: Bob's birthday is around the corner. I need your help to __________ some ideas so I can buy him a good gift.

explanation: Clue: the speaker wants help with 'some ideas' for a gift, so the friend is being asked to suggest ideas.
'put forward' means to suggest or offer an idea for others to consider.
'take up' means to start a hobby or to accept an offer; 'count on' means to depend on someone; 'see through' means to realise that someone is trying to trick you. None of them means to suggest.
The answer is option (3), put forward.

questions.stem: Choose the word closest in meaning to ++alleviate++.

explanation: 'alleviate' means to make something bad, such as pain or a problem, less severe.
Clue in the passage: the next sentence says petting a dog has an impact on 'reducing anxiety levels'. Companionship makes loneliness and stress less.
'reduce' means to make less, so it is the closest. 'intensify' is the opposite (make stronger).
'trim' and 'shorten' are tempting because they also make something smaller, but they are about cutting length or size, not about feelings. The answer is option (2).

questions.stem: Choose the word closest in meaning to ++regular++.

explanation: 'regular' walks are walks that happen often and at steady times, such as every day.
Clue in the passage: the walks 'encourage more physical activity', so they must happen often.
'frequent' means happening often, so it is the closest.
'occasional' (only sometimes) and 'random' (with no pattern) are the opposite idea, and 'casual' means relaxed. The answer is option (3).

questions.stem: Choose the word closest in meaning to ++anecdotes++.

explanation: An 'anecdote' is a short, interesting or funny story about something that really happened to you.
Clue in the passage: dog owners 'bond and connect' by telling one another about 'their dogs' quirky behaviours', that is, real things their dogs did.
A 'recount' is a retelling of something that happened, so it is the closest.

'fables' is tempting because fables are also short stories, but they are made-up stories with a moral. 'reports' are formal and factual, and 'testimonials' are statements praising a product or person. The answer is option (3).

questions.stem: Choose the words closest in meaning to ++no walk in the park++.

explanation: The idiom 'a walk in the park' means something very easy to do. So 'no walk in the park' means not easy at all.
Clue in the passage: the paragraph starts with 'However', turning from the benefits to the hard part, and says owners must 'commit to their needs for many years'.
'not demanding' means not needing much effort, which is the opposite. 'not rewarding' is wrong because the first paragraph lists many benefits.
The answer is option (1), not easy.

questions.stem: Choose the word closest in meaning to ++completely++.

explanation: 'completely' means totally, in every way, with nothing left out.
'fully' has the same meaning: 'fully prepared' = 'completely prepared'.
'adequately' is tempting, but it means only just enough, which is weaker than completely. 'basically' means in the main or simple points only, and 'exceptionally' means unusually or extremely well.
The answer is option (1), fully.

questions.stem: "Carry Everything in Style." The purpose of this statement in Text 1 is to __________.
options: highlight that the bag is useful and trendy
encourage students to be both well-prepared and stylish
remind students to look good while carrying their belongings

explanation: Break the slogan into its two halves. 'Carry Everything' says the bag holds all you need, so it is useful. 'in Style' says the bag looks good, so it is trendy.
A slogan on a poster advertises the product. Option (2) covers both halves and is about the bag.
Option (1) is tempting, but it covers only 'Carry Everything' and leaves out 'in Style'.
Options (3) and (4) are about what students should do; the slogan is selling the bag, not advising students. The answer is option (2).

review.note: The 'Text 1' heading above the poster is cut off at the top of the scanned page; the poster is taken as Text 1 because the next page is headed 'Text 2'. The group instruction is the one printed above Question 21.

questions.stem: How does Ansel's review in Text 1 reinforce the information presented in the poster?
options: It shows that the bag is suitable for all 12-year-olds.
It highlights the bag's spacious storage and comfort.
It emphasises that the sole appeal of the bag is its size.
It mentions a specific feature of the bag not shown in the poster.

explanation: 'Reinforce' means to support or repeat what the poster already says. Match Ansel's words to the poster.

Ansel: 'Everything I need for school fits inside it' matches 'Fit your entire school day into one bag' (spacious storage). 'it's extremely comfortable' matches 'Big bags never felt so comfortable!' (comfort).
(3) is wrong: he bought it for its comfort, so size is not the 'sole' (only) appeal. (1) is wrong: one boy's opinion cannot show it suits all 12-year-olds.
(4) is tempting because he says he can find any item easily, but the poster already says 'a specific space for everything', so it is not a new feature. The answer is option (2).

questions.stem:
Based on Text 1, which of the following statements are true about the Peaks school bags?
A: The bag is small and light.
B: The bag comes in different colours.
C: The bag has multiple compartments.

explanation: Check each statement against the poster.
A is false: the poster says 'Big bags never felt so comfortable!' and Ansel says 'it's bigger than other school bags'. Nothing says the bag is light.
B is true: 'Wide range of colours to choose from!'
C is true: 'Get organised with a specific space for everything!' Separate spaces for different things are compartments.
Only B and C are true. The answer is option (3).

questions.stem: What is the **main** message of Text 2?
options: Students should choose school bags with more features.
Students should use lockers or desks to store their belongings.
Students should prioritise comfort when choosing and using school bags.
Students should express their personality and personal style through their choice of school bags.

explanation: The main message is the idea that the whole text builds up to, not a single detail.

Paragraph 2 warns that a heavy bag 'strains your back' and tells you to 'carry a school bag that fits comfortably on your back' (choosing). Paragraph 3 tells you to pack 'only the items needed for the day' to 'protect your back' (using). Both are about comfort and protecting the back.
(2) is tempting, but lockers and desks are only an example ('For example, ...') of how to keep the bag light.

(4) is only the opening observation, which the writer then questions with 'have you considered the weight?'. (1) is wrong because the text names two helpful features, not 'more' features. The answer is option (3).

questions.stem: Texts 1 and 2 express differing views on whether __________.
options: students can store certain items in school
school bags should look appealing to students
school bags can fit everything needed for school
students should fit everything into their school bags

explanation: 'Differing views' means the two texts disagree. Find the point where one says yes and the other says no.
Text 1 encourages it: 'Fit your entire school day into one bag – all your books, stationery, lunch boxes and more!'
Text 2 discourages it: 'While it may seem exciting to fit everything into one bag, have you considered the weight?' and experts recommend 'packing only the items needed for the day'.

(3) is tempting, but Text 2 never says a bag **cannot** fit everything; it says you **should not** carry everything. The disagreement is about 'should'. (1) is only in Text 2, and both texts agree that bags look appealing. The answer is option (4).

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (26). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: After the blank is 'been learning', so the blank needs a helping verb that goes with 'been': have, has or had.

The visit happened 'Last Saturday' (past). The learning went on 'For months' **before** that visit. An action that continued up to a point in the past takes the past perfect continuous: had been + verb-ing.
(G) 'have' also makes a correct sentence if the members are still learning now ('have been learning'), and the key accepts both letters.
The answer is (F) had: 'the club members had been learning'. (G) have is also accepted.

review.note: The key accepts both F (had) and G (have). Solved first as G (have); F (had) fits the past-tense recount at least as well, so F is the displayed answer and both are accepted. Neither word is needed for another blank.

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (27). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: After the blank is the singular noun 'team', and the idea is that every one of the groups tried a different activity.
'each' is used before a singular noun to talk about every member of a group, one by one: 'each team'.
(A) 'another' also goes before a singular noun, but it means one more; it does not fit 'so that ___ team could try a **different** activity'.
The answer is (E) each.

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (28). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: The second half gives the reason for the first half. Why loosen the soil gently? The roots were delicate.
A connector that introduces a reason is 'because'.
The answer is (C) because: 'loosen the soil gently because the roots were delicate'.

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (29). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: The words after the blank ('was safer for children to use') tell us more about 'a tool with a short handle'.
To add information about a thing, use the relative pronoun 'which'. It also acts as the subject of 'was'.
The answer is (Q) which: 'a tool with a short handle which was safer for children to use'.

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (30). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: The blank comes between 'we' and 'not pour', so it needs a modal verb (a helping verb followed by the base form 'pour').
The farmer is giving a firm instruction about something they are not allowed to do. 'must not' is used to forbid something.
(K) 'shall' is also a modal, but 'shall not' is not used for giving this kind of instruction.
The answer is (H) must: 'we must not pour too much water onto the plants'.

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (31). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: Compare the two halves: 'Too little water would dry them out' and 'too much water would drown them'. They are opposite problems.
A connector that joins two contrasting ideas is 'but'.
The answer is (D) but.

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (32). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: '___ the end of the session' needs a preposition of time.
The fixed phrase is 'at the end of' something (at the end of the day, at the end of the lesson).
The blank starts the sentence, so it is written with a capital letter: 'At the end of the session'.
The answer is (B) at.

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (33). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: Before the blank is the comparative adjective 'heavier'.
Rule: comparative adjective + 'than' to compare two things: heavier than, taller than.
(M) 'then' looks and sounds similar, but 'then' is about time (next, after that). Do not mix them up.
The answer is (L) than: 'heavier than the rest'.

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (34). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: The blank comes before the noun 'hands', so it needs a possessive word that says whose hands.
The farmer 'told **us** to wash ___ hands'. The hands belong to 'us', and the possessive form for we/us is 'our'.
(N) 'their' is tempting, but the writer is part of the group ('we thanked the farmer', 'told us'), so it must be 'our', not 'their'.
The answer is (J) our.

questions.stem: Choose the most suitable word for blank (35). (Type its letter, A to Q.)

explanation: The second half tells us the time or condition under which fresh produce tastes better: it is eaten soon after harvesting.
'when' joins the two clauses and means 'at the time that' or 'whenever'.
(M) 'then' cannot join two clauses like this, and (C) 'because' is already used for blank (28).
The answer is (P) when: 'tastes better when it is eaten soon after harvesting'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (36) ++have++.

explanation: This is a grammar error. The subject is 'everyone'. Words like everyone, everybody and each are singular, so the plural verb 'have' is wrong.

Next choose the tense. The sentence reports what the teacher said in the past ('reminded us that...'), and the whole passage is a past-tense recount. In reported speech the verb moves back into the past: has becomes had.
Compare the next sentence, which is also reported speech in the past: 'She also said that a panel **would** be put...'.
The correct word is 'had'.

review.note: Solved first as 'has' (singular verb for 'everyone'). The key gives 'had', which is the better answer: the clause is reported speech after 'reminded' in a past-tense recount, matching 'would be put' in the next sentence. Only 'had' is accepted, as in the key; a marker might also accept 'has'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (37) ++comemoret++.

explanation: This is a spelling error. The word means to remember and show respect for an important person or event.
Say it in syllables: com-mem-o-rate. It has a double 'm' followed by a single 'm': co**mm**e**m**orate.
It ends in '-ate', like 'celebrate' and 'decorate'.
The correct word is 'commemorate'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (38) ++in++.

explanation: This is a grammar error: the wrong preposition.
The fixed phrase is 'buzzing **with** activity' (or 'buzzing with excitement'), meaning full of busy movement and noise.
Similar phrases also take 'with': filled with, bursting with, crowded with.
The correct word is 'with'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (39) ++were++.

explanation: This is a grammar error in subject-verb agreement.
The subject is 'Every display board'. Rule: 'every' and 'each' are followed by a singular noun and a singular verb.
The sentence is in the past tense ('before the visitors arrived'), so the singular past form is 'was'.
The correct word is 'was': 'Every display board was checked very carefully'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (40) ++coherant++.

explanation: This is a spelling error. The word means clear, well organised and easy to understand.
Say it in syllables: co-her-ent. The ending is '-ent', not '-ant'.
It belongs with other '-ent' words such as 'different', 'excellent' and 'confident'.
The correct word is 'coherent'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (41) ++wrote++.

explanation: This is a grammar error. Look at the helping verb in front: 'he **had** ___'.
Rule: had + past participle makes the past perfect tense. 'wrote' is the simple past form; the past participle of 'write' is 'written' (write, wrote, written).
The past perfect fits because he wrote about the place 'many years earlier', before he told the pupils.
The correct word is 'written'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (42) ++jornal++.

explanation: This is a spelling error. The word means a book in which you write about what happens to you, like a diary.
The first syllable is spelt 'jour', with 'ou', as in 'journey'.
j-o-u-r-n-a-l.
The correct word is 'journal'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (43) ++asppecialy++.

explanation: This is a spelling error. The word means particularly or very.
It is the word 'special' with 'e' in front and '-ly' at the end: e + special + ly.
So it begins with 'e' (not 'a'), has one 'p', and has a double 'l' because 'special' ends in 'l' and we add 'ly'.
The correct word is 'especially'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (44) ++Since++.

explanation: This is a grammar error: the wrong connector.

Look at the meaning. They were tired, yet they still felt the effort was worthwhile. The two ideas contrast, so we need a word that means 'even though'. 'Since' gives a reason, which does not make sense here.

The word must also fit the grammar: it is followed by 'being tired' (an -ing form). 'Despite' is followed by a noun or an -ing form: 'Despite being tired'. 'Although' would need a full clause ('Although we were tired').
The correct word is 'Despite'.

questions.stem: Write the correct word for (45) ++undoubtably++.

explanation: This is a spelling error. The word means certainly, without any doubt.
Build it up: doubt, undoubted, undoubted + ly. The ending is '-edly', not '-ably'.
Remember the silent 'b' in 'doubt'.
The correct word is 'undoubtedly'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (46) with a suitable word.

explanation: The sentence compares the old way ('copying notes for the entire period') with the new way ('students now work in small groups').
The blank is followed by 'of' + an -ing word. The phrase 'Instead of' + verb-ing means 'in place of' doing something.
It starts the sentence, so it takes a capital letter.
The answer is 'Instead'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (47) with a suitable word.

explanation: The students work together 'to answer questions, sort cards and explain ideas to one another', so they are in small sets of people.
Look ahead for the same idea: 'They can first discuss in small **groups** before speaking to the whole class.'
The noun must be plural because there is no 'a' before 'small'. 'teams' also fits.
The answer is 'groups'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (48) with a suitable word.

explanation: Students must 'think carefully about ___ their ideas make sense to others'. They are checking: do my ideas make sense, or not?
'whether' introduces a yes-or-no question inside a sentence, and it can follow a preposition such as 'about'.
'if' is tempting, but we do not use 'if' straight after a preposition ('about if' is wrong). 'how' also makes a sensible sentence.
The answer is 'whether'.

review.note: 'how' is added to the accept list as it is clearly correct in context ('think carefully about how their ideas make sense to others'); the key gives only 'whether'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (49) with a suitable word.

explanation: After the small-group talk, the students tell their answers ('them') to 'the class'.
The verb must go with 'with': we **share** something **with** someone.
After the preposition 'before', the verb takes the -ing form: 'before sharing them'.
The answer is 'sharing'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (50) with a suitable word.

explanation: The blank is the subject of 'gives them time to build their confidence'. What gives them time? The whole idea in the sentence before: discussing in small groups first.
To point back to a whole idea that has just been mentioned, use 'This'.
The verb 'gives' is singular, so a plural word like 'These' or 'They' is wrong.
The answer is 'This'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (51) with a suitable word.

explanation: Clue cards are arranged 'to show how a process works'. A process has steps that happen one after another.
The phrase is 'in the correct order', meaning each step is in its right place. 'sequence' means the same.
The answer is 'order'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (52) with a suitable word.

explanation: Students earn points by doing something about 'why one answer is wrong while another is correct'. Giving the reason why is explaining.
Look back for the same idea: students 'explain ideas to one another' in the first paragraph.
After the preposition 'by', the verb takes the -ing form: 'by explaining'.
The answer is 'explaining'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (53) with a suitable word.

explanation: The sentence tells us a change teachers have noticed 'after taking part in such activities', so it compares students now with students before.
The whole passage is positive about the games (quieter students join in and build confidence), so the students are 'more willing' to ask questions, not less.
'willing' is a long adjective, so its comparative is formed with 'more'.
The answer is 'more'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (54) with a suitable word.

explanation: The pattern after the blank is noun + base verb: '___ learning feel less stressful'. The verb that fits this pattern is 'make': make + something + do something.
The same pattern appears in the last sentence: 'revision games can **make** learning enjoyable'.
The subject 'the games' is plural and the paragraph is in the present tense, so we write 'make', not 'makes' or 'made'.
The answer is 'make'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (55) with a suitable word.

explanation: 'Of course' introduces a condition: the games help **only** on the condition that students still revise and do their homework.
'only if' introduces the one condition that must be met.
The answer is 'if': 'beneficial only if students continue to revise their notes'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (56) with a suitable word.

explanation: The blank comes after two groups, 'teachers and students', and before the verb 'should understand'.
'A and B alike' means both A and B equally. It is placed after the two nouns: 'teachers and students alike'.
'both' is tempting, but it normally comes before the pair ('both teachers and students'), not in this position.
The answer is 'alike'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (57) with a suitable word.

explanation: The clause needs a verb: 'the use of such activities in lessons ___ just one part of the learning process'.
Find the true subject. It is 'the use', not 'activities' or 'lessons', which only belong to the phrases after 'of' and 'in'. 'the use' is singular.
The paragraph is in the present tense, so the singular present verb is 'is'. 'are' is the trap.
The answer is 'is'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (58) with a suitable word.

explanation: 'time set ___ for reading, practice and discussion' is about keeping some time for a special purpose.
The phrasal verb 'set aside' means to keep or save something, especially time or money, for a purpose.
The answer is 'aside': 'with time set aside for reading, practice and discussion'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (59) with a suitable word.

explanation: 'more often than ___' is a fixed phrase.
'more often than not' means usually, or most of the time.
So a balanced routine is usually the most effective way to prepare for an examination.
The answer is 'not'.

questions.stem: Fill in blank (60) with a suitable word.

explanation: 'stay ___ task' is a fixed phrase.
To 'stay on task' means to keep your attention on the work you are supposed to be doing.
It fits the meaning: students who enjoy learning are more likely to keep working.
The answer is 'on'.

questions.stem:
The rain stopped. The players continued with the match immediately.
No sooner ____________________.
(Rewrite as one sentence using the word(s) given. The meaning must stay the same.)

answer.value: No sooner had the rain stopped than the players continued with the match.
accept: No sooner had the rain stopped than the players continued with the match immediately.

explanation: 'No sooner ... than ...' shows that the second action happened straight after the first.
When a sentence begins with 'No sooner', the helping verb comes before the subject (inversion), and the first action is in the past perfect: No sooner **had** the rain **stopped** ...
The second action follows 'than' (not 'when' or 'then') and stays in the simple past: ... than the players continued with the match.
Drop 'immediately', because 'No sooner' already carries that meaning. Answer: No sooner had the rain stopped than the players continued with the match.

review.keyAnswer: No sooner had the rain stopped than the players continued with the match.
review.solvedAnswer: No sooner had the rain stopped than the players continued with the match.

questions.stem:
Mr Bala invited the artist to speak at the assembly. Her painting had won first prize.
____________________ whose ____________________.
(Rewrite as one sentence using the word(s) given. The meaning must stay the same.)

answer.value: Mr Bala invited the artist whose painting had won first prize to speak at the assembly.

explanation: 'whose' is the relative pronoun that shows belonging. It replaces 'Her' in the second sentence: 'Her painting' becomes 'whose painting'.
The 'whose' clause must come straight after the noun it describes, 'the artist': ... the artist whose painting had won first prize ...
Then finish the first sentence: ... to speak at the assembly. Do not put the clause at the end ('...at the assembly whose painting...'), or it will seem to describe the assembly.
Keep the tenses: 'invited' and 'had won'. Answer: Mr Bala invited the artist whose painting had won first prize to speak at the assembly.

review.keyAnswer: Mr Bala invited the artist whose painting had won first prize to speak at the assembly.
review.solvedAnswer: Mr Bala invited the artist whose painting had won first prize to speak at the assembly.

questions.stem:
Tommy is writing several articles for the school newsletter.
Several articles ____________________.
(Rewrite as one sentence using the word(s) given. The meaning must stay the same.)

answer.value: Several articles are being written by Tommy for the school newsletter.
accept: Several articles for the school newsletter are being written by Tommy.

explanation: The sentence now starts with the object, 'Several articles', so it must change from active to passive voice.
Keep the same tense. 'is writing' is the present continuous; its passive form is am/is/are + being + past participle.
'Several articles' is plural, so use 'are': are being written. The past participle of 'write' is 'written'.
Add the doer with 'by': by Tommy. Answer: Several articles are being written by Tommy for the school newsletter.

review.keyAnswer: Several articles are being written by Tommy for the school newsletter.
review.solvedAnswer: Several articles are being written by Tommy for the school newsletter.

questions.stem:
Lisa asked Ben if he had managed to complete all his homework the previous week.
Lisa asked Ben, "____________________?"
(Rewrite as one sentence using the word(s) given. The meaning must stay the same.)

answer.value: Lisa asked Ben, "Did you manage to complete all your homework last week?"
accept: Did you manage to complete all your homework last week?
Did you manage to complete all your homework last week

explanation: This changes reported speech back into direct speech, so undo each change that reporting makes.

Tense: move one step forward. The past perfect 'had managed' becomes the simple past. In a question that is 'Did ... manage', and 'if' is dropped because a direct yes/no question starts with the helping verb.
Pronouns: Lisa is speaking to Ben, so 'he' becomes 'you' and 'his' becomes 'your'.
Time: 'the previous week' becomes 'last week'. End with a question mark inside the quotation marks. Answer: Lisa asked Ben, "Did you manage to complete all your homework last week?"

review.keyAnswer: Lisa asked Ben, "Did you manage to complete all your homework last week?"
review.solvedAnswer: Lisa asked Ben, "Did you manage to complete all your homework last week?"
review.note: The end of the key's line (after 'homework') is partly under the watermark; 'last week?"' can still be made out.

questions.stem:
Mrs Lee had such confidence in her team that she did not supervise them at all.
So ____________________.
(Rewrite as one sentence using the word(s) given. The meaning must stay the same.)

answer.value: So confident was Mrs Lee in her team that she did not supervise them at all.
accept: So much confidence did Mrs Lee have in her team that she did not supervise them at all.

explanation: 'such' is followed by a noun (such confidence), but 'so' is followed by an adjective. Change the noun 'confidence' to the adjective 'confident'.
When a sentence begins with 'So + adjective', the verb comes before the subject (inversion): So confident **was Mrs Lee** ... (not 'So confident Mrs Lee was').
Because the noun has become an adjective, 'had' changes to the verb 'to be' in the same tense: was.
Keep the rest: ... in her team that she did not supervise them at all. Answer: So confident was Mrs Lee in her team that she did not supervise them at all.

review.keyAnswer: So confident was Mrs Lee in her team that she did not supervise them at all.
review.solvedAnswer: So confident was Mrs Lee in her team that she did not supervise them at all.
review.note: The end of the key's line is partly under the watermark but readable. 'So much confidence did Mrs Lee have in her team that...' is added to the accept list as an equally correct inversion.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph one, which **three-word phrase** shows how the narrator felt after the teacher's comment?

explanation: Find the sentence in paragraph 1 that tells us how she felt afterwards: 'For the rest of the day, I carried a quiet heaviness in me'.
'heaviness' here is a feeling, not a weight: she felt sad and weighed down by the teacher's words. 'quiet' shows she kept the hurt to herself.
Count exactly three words and copy them without changing anything: a (1) quiet (2) heaviness (3). Writing more or fewer words loses the mark.
The answer is 'a quiet heaviness'.

questions.stem:
What does the phrase "turn themselves into the shape the school wanted" in lines 6-7 (paragraph 2, from "Everyone around me" to "school wanted") suggest about the students? Tick the correct answer.
compliant / empathetic / flexible
(Type compliant, empathetic or flexible.)

explanation: Read the sentence before the phrase: pupils were 'supposed to line up neatly, socks pulled up, hair tied properly, badges pinned straight'. These are the school's rules.
'The shape the school wanted' means the way the school expected pupils to look and behave. The others knew how to fit that shape, so they followed the rules. The writer, 'unlike the others', did not.
'compliant' means willing to obey rules and do what you are told, so it matches.

'flexible' is tempting because of the word 'shape', but it means able to change easily to suit new situations, which is not the same as obeying. 'empathetic' means able to understand other people's feelings. The answer is 'compliant'.

review.keyAnswer: (No box is ticked in the key.)
review.note: The answer key prints the three choices for Q67 but none of the boxes is ticked, so there is no key answer to compare with. 'compliant' is the solved answer and is certain from the context: the phrase follows the list of dress rules that everyone except the writer obeyed.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, state **two** ways in which the writer's attire was different from the other students.

parts.label: a

answer.value: Her shirt was tucked out. (Any two of these three: her shirt was tucked out; her shoes were dirty; her shoelaces were two different shades of blue.)
accept: She had her shirt tucked out.

explanation: 'Attire' means what a person wears: clothes and shoes.

Find the sentence that begins 'I, unlike the others, ...'. The words 'unlike the others' tell you this is where she was different: 'had my shirt tucked out and dirty shoes. My shoelaces were two different shades of blue'.
That gives three possible answers: shirt tucked out, dirty shoes, shoelaces of two different shades of blue. Write one here and a different one in (b).
Change 'my' to 'her': Her shirt was tucked out.

parts.label: b

answer.value: Her shoes were dirty. (Or: her shoelaces were two different shades of blue. It must be a different point from your first answer.)
accept: Her shoelaces were two different shades of blue.

explanation: Give a second, different point from the same sentences: 'dirty shoes' or 'My shoelaces were two different shades of blue'.
Do not write about the drawing on the newsletter. That is behaviour, not attire.
Do not copy the rules ('socks pulled up, hair tied properly'); those describe the other students, not the writer.
Answer: Her shoes were dirty (or: Her shoelaces were two different shades of blue).

review.keyAnswer: 1. Her shirt was tucked out. 2. Her shoelaces were two different shades of blue. 3. Her shoes were dirty. (Any two of the three above.)
review.solvedAnswer: Shirt tucked out; dirty shoes; shoelaces of two different shades of blue (any two). Agrees with key.

questions.stem: Why did the writer feel that things were not easy with her mother?

answer.value: Her mother often scolded her (for not doing what she was told) and compared her with her cousin, who knew how to behave.

explanation: The question words 'not easy' match the start of paragraph 4: 'At home, things were not much easier.' The reasons follow straight after.
Point 1 (1 mark): '"Can you do what you are told?" Mother often scolded.' Her mother often scolded her.
Point 2 (1 mark): '"Why can't you be more like your cousin? She knows how to behave."' Her mother compared her with her cousin.
The question is worth 2 marks, so give both points in your own sentence instead of copying the speech: Her mother often scolded her and compared her with her cousin.

review.keyAnswer: The writer's mother often scolded her [the key prints 'her mother', a typing slip] and compared her with her cousin.
review.solvedAnswer: Her mother often scolded her and compared her with her cousin. Agrees with key.
review.note: The key's sentence reads 'The writer's mother often scolded her mother and compared her with her cousin'; the second 'mother' is a typing slip. Part of the line is under the watermark but readable.

questions.stem: Based on paragraphs 2 to 7, state whether each statement in the table below is true or false, then give one reason why you think so.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt:
The teacher approved of the writer's drawing on the newsletter.
(Type True or False, then give one reason from the passage.)

answer.value: False. The teacher questioned her sharply about the drawing (and said that it showed what her problem was).

explanation: Find the drawing in paragraph 2: the writer 'had been **caught** drawing a strange shape in the margin of the school newsletter instead of reading it'.

The teacher's reaction: '"What is that?" my form teacher had asked **sharply**', and then 'That is your problem.' To approve of something is to think it is good; a sharp question and a criticism show the opposite.
So the statement is False. The reason must be evidence from the passage: the teacher asked about it sharply.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt:
The writer had planned to contribute to the script-writing from the beginning.
(Type True or False, then give one reason from the passage.)

answer.value: False. The writer had never imagined herself taking over the script; the words slipped out before she could stop herself.

explanation: Find the script-writing in paragraph 5. 'I **suddenly** felt something stir inside me. **Before I could stop myself**, the words slipped out.' This was sudden, not planned.
The clearest evidence: 'This was something I never imagined myself doing.' You cannot plan something you never imagined doing.
So the statement is False. Reason: she had never imagined herself writing (taking over) the script.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt:
The audience were entertained by the performance.
(Type True or False, then give one reason from the passage.)

answer.value: True. The audience laughed at the right moments.

explanation: Find the performance in paragraph 6: 'During the performance, the audience laughed at the right moments.'
The writer had made the dialogue 'sharper and funnier', so laughing at the right moments shows the audience enjoyed it. 'Entertained' means amused and interested.
So the statement is True. Reason: the audience laughed at the right moments.

review.keyAnswer: a) False: The teacher questioned her sharply. b) False: The writer had never imagined herself writing a script. c) True: The audience laughed at the right moments.
review.solvedAnswer: a) False (asked sharply; 'That is your problem'); b) False (never imagined herself doing it; words slipped out); c) True (audience laughed at the right moments). Agrees with key.
review.note: The statements in the key's table are partly under the watermark; the True/False column and the reasons are clear.

questions.stem:
Look at the amoeba traits in the table below. Complete the table to compare what the teacher thought of the writer at the beginning of the story with what the writer thought of herself at the end.
[[table1]]

header: Teacher's view of the writer (at the start of the story)
Writer's view of herself (at the end of the story)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: No proper shape: the writer's view of herself (at the end of the story)

answer.value: Adaptable (she could adapt and change; she was still forming, not broken).

explanation: The end of the story is paragraph 8, where she draws the amoeba again: 'this time, I saw a creature that **could adapt** and find its own way forward.'

'Find its own way forward' is already used in the table ('Finding her own path') for 'Float around'. So 'could adapt' is the one that matches 'No proper shape': something with no fixed shape can change to suit what is around it.
She adds: 'not fitting in did not mean I was broken; it simply meant I was still forming.' She now sees having no fixed shape as a strength.
The answer is adaptable (able to adapt).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Float around: the teacher's view of the writer (at the start of the story)

answer.value: Aimless (she had no aim, direction or purpose).

explanation: The teacher's view is in paragraph 2: 'A single-celled organism with no proper shape. Just floating about **aimlessly**. That is your problem.'
The teacher linked 'floating about' with 'aimlessly', which means without any aim, purpose or direction.

parts.prompt: How the writer felt when the English teacher approached her and asked if she had written most of the performance:

answer.value: Nervous (she was expecting to be criticised).

explanation: Find the event in paragraph 6: '"You wrote most of that, didn't you?" she asked. I nodded, **expecting criticism**.'
The table wants a feeling, not a quotation. If you expect to be criticised, you feel nervous or worried about what is coming.
Remember her past: teachers had only ever singled her out for being 'wrong', so she expected the same again.
The answer is nervous (anxious, worried and apprehensive mean the same).

explanation: Find the loudest girl in paragraph 7: 'One of them, the loudest in the group, smiled awkwardly and **asked if I would help her with her drama club audition** the following week.'
The table says she felt 'impressed', and the passage says she now looked at the writer 'not as a joke, but as an expert'. Asking for help is the action that shows this.
Change 'I' to 'the writer'. 'Smiled awkwardly' alone is not enough; the important action is asking for help.
The answer is: She asked the writer to help her with her drama club audition.

answer.value: The school newsletter (in whose margin the writer had drawn the amoeba).

explanation: Read the sentence just before: 'I had been caught drawing a strange shape in the margin of **the school newsletter** instead of reading it.'
Then: '"What is that?" my form teacher had asked sharply, holding up **my paper**.' The teacher held up the thing the writer had been drawing on.
Test by replacing the words: 'holding up the school newsletter' makes sense.
The answer is the school newsletter.

parts.label: b

answer.value: Rewriting the script (the whole scene) for the class performance.

explanation: Read the sentence just before: 'I began **rewriting the whole scene**. In half an hour, I completed **the task**.'
The task she completed is the thing she had just begun: rewriting the scene, that is, the script she had taken over.
'Creating the short performance' is tempting, but that was the whole class's job and it was not finished in half an hour. 'The task' is her own job of rewriting.
The answer is rewriting the script (the whole scene).

questions.stem: Explain clearly why the writer's classmates "groaned and did the bare minimum" (line 29, paragraph 5) for the short performance?

answer.value: They did not want to do the performance (their fun of playing board games, gossiping and laughing had been interrupted), and they only wanted to get it over with.

explanation: Split the phrase in two, because there are 2 marks. Why did they groan? Why did they do only the bare minimum?

'groaned' (1 mark): a groan shows you are unhappy about something. They were 'engrossed in playing board games, gossiping and laughing' when this 'was interrupted' by the teacher's instructions. They did not want to do the performance.

'did the bare minimum' (1 mark): this means doing as little as possible. The next sentence explains why: 'they argued lazily over the script, **hoping to get it over with**'. They just wanted to finish it quickly.
Answer: They did not want to do the performance and wanted to get it over with.

review.keyAnswer: They did not want to do the project (1m) and wanted to get it over with (1m).
review.solvedAnswer: They were unwilling to do the performance, which interrupted their fun, and just wanted to get it over with. Agrees with key.

questions.stem: Explain clearly what the writer hoped to achieve by writing and directing plays.

answer.value: She hoped that her plays would reach someone like her who did not fit in, and let that person know that she was not alone.

explanation: The answer is in the last two sentences of paragraph 8: 'I began to imagine myself writing and directing plays. Maybe one day, these would reach a fellow amoeba who needed to know that she was not alone.'

Point 1 (1 mark): to reach 'a fellow amoeba'. This is not a real amoeba. In this story 'amoeba' stands for a person who does not fit in, so 'a fellow amoeba' is someone like the writer. You must explain this instead of copying the words.
Point 2 (1 mark): to let that person know that she is not alone.
Answer: She hoped to reach someone like her who did not fit in, and let that person know that she was not alone.

review.keyAnswer: She hoped to reach out to someone like her (1m) and let the person know that she was not alone (1m).
review.solvedAnswer: To reach others who, like her, did not fit in, and let them know they were not alone. Agrees with key.
